question: What status code should the endpoint DELETE /api/users/:id return on successful deletion?

options.text: 204 No Content -- successful deletion, no response body needed
410 Gone -- the resource no longer exists
options.explanation: 410 Gone means the resource once existed but has been permanently removed. This is not a success response code for DELETE, but an informational status for future GET requests

options.text: 202 Accepted -- deletion has been queued for processing
options.explanation: 202 is used for asynchronous operations (queued). For synchronous deletion the correct answer is 204 No Content

options.text: 200 OK with body { deleted: true }
options.explanation: 200 OK is acceptable, but 204 No Content is the standard practice for DELETE. The client does not need a response body: it knows the resource was deleted by the status code

question: Why is cursor-based pagination more stable than offset-based during concurrent inserts?

options.text: Cursor points to a specific record (WHERE id > N), while offset counts from the beginning -- an insert shifts all subsequent pages
Cursor-based pagination locks the table from inserts
options.explanation: Cursor-based does not lock the table. Stability is achieved by anchoring to a specific value (id > 40) rather than a positional number (OFFSET 40)

options.text: Cursor caches the result on the server
options.explanation: Cursor does not cache the result -- it stores a position (usually an ID). Stability comes from WHERE id > 40 returning the same next records regardless of inserts at the beginning

options.text: Offset-based is slower and therefore skips records
options.explanation: Speed is not the cause of skips. The problem is that OFFSET 40 shifts when a new record is inserted: record #40 becomes #41, and the user sees it twice or misses it

question: How should you correctly implement multi-field sorting in a REST API?

options.text: ?orderBy=createdAt DESC, name ASC (SQL syntax)
options.explanation: SQL syntax in query params is dangerous (SQL injection), hard to parse, and non-standard. Use sort=-createdAt,name

options.text: ?sort={"createdAt":"desc","name":"asc"}
options.explanation: JSON in query params is hard to read, encode, and cache. The convention sort=-field1,field2 is simpler and widely supported

options.text: ?sort=-createdAt,name -- comma-separated fields, minus means DESC
?sortBy=createdAt&sortOrder=DESC&sortBy2=name&sortOrder2=ASC
options.explanation: Numbered parameters (sortBy2, sortOrder2) are inconvenient and do not scale. The standard convention is: sort=-field1,field2 -- compact and extensible

question: Which API versioning approach is the most popular and why?

options.text: No versioning needed -- backward compatibility is sufficient
options.explanation: Backward compatibility is ideal but unrealistic for major changes (renaming fields, restructuring). Versioning is a necessary tool

options.text: Content negotiation (Accept header) -- follows HTTP standards
options.explanation: Content negotiation is the most spec-correct approach but harder to use: complex Accept header, harder to debug. URL versioning wins on simplicity

options.text: URL versioning (/api/v1/) -- simple, clear, easy to cache and proxy
Header versioning (X-API-Version) -- does not pollute the URL
options.explanation: Header versioning is valid but less popular: the version is not visible in the URL, harder to test in a browser and document. URL versioning is simpler for most teams

question: Which headers should be sent when deprecating an API version?

options.text: Sunset: <date> -- the date after which the version will stop working
Deprecation: true -- signal that the version is deprecated
X-Deprecated-Since: <date> -- non-standard header with a date
options.explanation: X-Deprecated-Since is a non-standard header. Use the standard ones: Deprecation (RFC 8594) and Sunset (RFC 8594) to notify clients

options.text: Link: </api/v2/users>; rel="successor-version" -- link to the new version
This approach is deprecated and no longer used
options.explanation: This approach is actively used in modern systems.
